stem:
Isha builds an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles. She peels it into $n$ nested L-shaped layers: the outermost L uses $2n-1$ tiles, then $2n-3$, and so on down to $1$.

Why does the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equal $n^{2}$?

options.text: Any collection of odd numbers sums to a square, even if the odds are not the first $n$ consecutive odds starting at $1$.
The same L-layer story also explains the up-and-down sum of ordinary counting numbers, so that sum must equal $n^{2}$ too.
The $n$-by-$n$ square can be partitioned into those $n$ nested odd L-layers, so $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^{2}$.
The answer is "odd numbers", because that phrase is printed most often in the problem.

teacher.key_rationale: An n-by-n square splits into n nested L-layers of sizes 1, 3, …, 2n−1, so the first n odd numbers sum to n². The odds must be consecutive from 1; the counting-number sum is a different hinge; the printed word "odd" is not the reason.
